title.en: Shenrab Miwo, Founder of the Bon
title.zh: 雍仲苯教創立者辛饒米沃

region.en: Land of Zhang-zhung, the old Bon heartland (symbolic pin at Mount Kailash)
region.zh: 古老苯教腹地象雄（以岡仁波齊為象徵定位）

texts.period: Bon sutra (Gtsang-ma klu hbum dkar-po, the Holy White Naga Hundred-thousand); German trans. Schiefner, English summary in Rockhill 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VII, summarizing A. Schiefner's translation of the Bon-po sutra

summary.en: The founder of the Bon religion, Shenrab Miwo, the excellent and glorious Mahapurusha 'whose compassion shines forth like the rays of the sun', holds in his right hand the iron hook of mercy with which he fishes people out of the ocean of transmigration - a hooked cross like the gyung-drung (swastika) that gives the creed its name. As a bodhisattva he obtained perfect freedom by walking the way of perfect charity, and took the form of the holy white Naga Hundred-thousand to teach the holy law through the ten regions of the thousand millions of continents.
summary.zh: 苯教祖師辛饒米沃，尊號「尊勝與榮耀之大人」，悲心如日光普照；右手持「慈悲鐵鉤」，自輪迴海中鉤出眾生——此鉤形如萬字（雍仲），苯教之名即由此而來。他自言宿世為菩薩，修布施波羅蜜而得自在，並化身「聖白龍十萬」於十方百俱胝洲教化眾生。

sensitivity.note: The Bon tradition is a living religion; paraphrase of public-domain summaries only; nothing restricted reproduced.

passages.text: The founder of the Bon-pa religion was Gshen-rabs, or Gshen-rabs mi-bo, called also excellent Mahapurusha, glorious Mahapurusha, whose compassion shines forth like the rays of the sun; in his right hand he holds the iron hook of mercy, and in his left the mudra of equality; on his head is the mitra jewel. It may possibly be that this iron hook of mercy, with which Gshen-rabs fishes people out of the ocean of transmigration, has something to do with the swastika cross, which is also a hooked cross.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), summarizing Schiefner's Bon sutra; not verbatim.

passages.text: In former times, as a bodhisattva, he says, I have obtained perfect freedom by walking in the way of perfect charity; and he took upon himself the task of teaching the holy law to all humanity in the ten regions of the thousand millions of continents, for which purpose he took the form of the holy white Naga Hundred-thousand. He taught the four truths of Gshen-rabs, the five perfections - charity, morality, patience, steadfastness and meditation - the five exoteric perfections, and the nine branches of the gyung-drung: in all the 142 rules of deliverance which are the foundation and root for humanity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Nyatri Tsenpo, First King of Tibet

region.en: Yarlung valley, the cradle of the Tibetan monarchy (symbolic pin at the Yarlung valley, Tibet)
region.zh: 雅礱谷地——吐蕃王統發祥地（以雅礱谷為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan royal chronicles (Bodhimur; reigned traditionally from 416 or 313 BC); Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VII

summary.en: The first king of Tibet, Chiya-khri Tsenpo - Nyatri Tsenpo - is claimed in Tibetan historiography as a son of King Prasenajit of Kosala, the Buddha's lifelong friend; twelve chiefs of the tribes of Southern and Central Tibet elected him in the hope of ending the internecine wars ravaging the country. He settled in the Yarlung country and built the castle of Phyi-dbang-stag-stse, known as the Ombo-blang-gang, ruled according to law, organized an army, and was glorified by the five principal sages in records of gold and turquoises.
summary.zh: 吐蕃首王聶赤贊普，藏文史書稱其為佛陀終身摯友、拘薩羅波斯匿王之子；吐蕃中部南部十二部酋長共舉之，冀止內亂。定都雅礱，建雍布拉康城堡，依法而治，整軍護土衛疆，五大智者以金與綠松石為之記功——如結繩記事之遺風。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material of the living Tibetan nation; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The first king of Tibet was Chiya-khri Tsenpo, a son of King Prasenadjit of Kosala; he was elected by the twelve chiefs of the tribes of Southern and Central Tibet, who hoped by this means to put an end to the internecine wars which were ravaging the country. He took up his residence in the Yarlung country and built a castle at Phyi-dbang-stag-stse, which became known as the U-bu bla-sgang or Ombo-blang-gang; he ruled according to law and the kingdom was in happiness, and he organised an army to protect his person, to quell troubles in the country and to keep off foreign enemies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The five principal sages glorified the king in records in gold and turquoises - a remark which seems to confirm what the Chinese say about the Tibetans making use of a species of quippus. Tibetan historians, in the reign of Ral-pa-chan, deliberately carried the genealogy of their monarchs back, if not to the Buddha himself, at least to one of his friends and protectors: as in Europe families are proud to claim descent from the Virgin Mary, so the first Tibetan monarch claims descent from Prasenajit, the life-long friend of the Buddha Gautama.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Seven Celestial Kings and the Tiger-Haired King

region.en: Yarlung dynasty seats, central Tibet (symbolic pin in the Yarlung valley)
region.zh: 雅礱王統諸都（以雅礱谷為象徵定位）

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VII

summary.en: Nyatri Tsenpo and his six successors are the 'seven celestial Khri', whose corpses were carried off to heaven when they died - a rule Rockhill compares with the twelve celestial sovereigns of the Chinese San Hwang. The next six are the 'six terrestrial Legs', and the fourth, Spu-de gung-rgyal 'the tiger-haired king', is the culture-hero of Tibetan crafts: in his reign charcoal and wells were first made, iron, copper and silver ore smelted, and ploughs introduced into the country.
summary.zh: 聶赤贊普及以下六王合稱「天赤七王」——死後屍身皆「自往天界」（其俗近於漢之三皇）；繼之為「地列六王」。其中第四位普德貢傑，號「虎衣王」，為吐蕃百工之祖：其世始用木炭、始鑿井、冶鐵銅銀礦，並引入耕犁。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: This king and his six successors are known as the seven celestial Khri; when they died their corpses were carried off to heaven - an analogy which may be found with the twelve celestial sovereigns of the San Hwang of the Chinese, just as the next series of six Tibetan kings, known as the six terrestrial Legs, resemble the eleven terrestrial sovereigns of the Chinese.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fourth king among the six terrestrial Legs was Spu-de gung-rgyal, the tiger-haired king, in whose reign charcoal and wells were first made, iron, copper and silver ore were smelted, and ploughs were introduced into the country - and we can imagine from this in what a savage state the Tibetans must have lived prior to this reign, the discoveries probably resulting from intercourse with the Chinese.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Casket from Heaven in the Reign of Lhathothori
title.zh: 拉妥妥日年贊時的天降寶篋

region.en: Royal palace at Ombu, central Tibet (symbolic pin at Yarlung)
region.zh: 藏中雍布拉康王宮（以雅礱為象徵定位）

texts.period: Reign of Lha-tho-tho-ri snyan-shal (traditionally 4th-5th century AD); Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VII

summary.en: In Lhathothori's eightieth year a casket fell from heaven into his palace, containing a copy of the Za-ma-thog bkod-pai mdo (Karandavyuha sutra), an alms-bowl, the six essential syllables Om mani padme hum, a golden chaitya and a clay image of the chintamani. A few years later five strangers came and explained their use and power, but the king, too deep-set in national superstition, honoured the casket with offerings as a fetish and did not embrace their religious ideas - so the first attempt at conversion failed and the strangers departed.
summary.zh: 拉妥妥日年贊王八十歲時，一寶篋自天降於王宮：內有《寶篋經》、一缽、「六字真言」、金塔一尊、如意寶泥像一軀。數年後五位異人入藏解其妙用，然王迷信深固，唯以寶篋為神物供養，未納其教——初傳佛法就此失敗，異人離去。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: While he was at Ombu in his eightieth year, there fell from heaven into his palace a casket which contained a copy of the Za-ma-thog bkod-pai mdo (Karandavyuha sutra), an alms-bowl, the six essential syllables (Om mani padme hum), a golden chaitya and a clay image of the chintamani; it is remarkable that the Karandavyuha sutra, not especially venerated in China or India, was one of the favourite books of the Nepalese - one of the reasons Rockhill suggests Buddhism first came to Tibet from Nepal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: A few years after the apparition in Tibet of these objects of Buddhist worship, five strangers came to the king and explained their use and power; but this first attempt at conversion proved unsuccessful, for the king, most likely imbued with national superstition too deep-set to be easily dispelled, had all kinds of honours and offerings made to the precious casket as if it were a fetish, but did not embrace the religious ideas of the strangers, who departed from the country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Thonmi Sambhota Invents the Tibetan Letters

region.en: Southern India, school of the Brahman Li-byin (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南印度黎賓婆羅門學塾（象徵定位）

texts.period: Reign of Srong-btsan sgam-po (third year of his reign, traditionally 616 AD); Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VII

summary.en: Srong-btsan sgam-po's first mission of seven nobles failed to find the route to India; in the third year of his reign he sent Thonmi Sambhota with sixteen companions, who overcame great difficulties on the road. In Southern India Thonmi learnt the Indian characters from the Brahman Li-byin and the pundit Singhaghosha, took twenty-four characters with slight alterations, invented six new ones for sounds the Indian language lacked, and formed the Tibetan capital alphabet, the Ka-phreng dbu-chan - and before returning he translated the Karandavyuha and Avalokiteshvara sutras and carried back a large collection of religious works.
summary.zh: 松贊干布初遣七貴族赴印度求字，未能得路而返；第三年再遣吞彌·桑布扎攜十六人前往。吞彌於南印度從黎賓婆羅門與僧伽霍沙習字，取二十四字母略加改易，另創六個印度語所無之字母，遂成藏文三十字母（哇欽）；歸國前又譯《寶篋經》《觀音經》等多部經典，攜大量佛書返藏。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: One of Srong-btsan's first preoccupations was to form an alphabet for the Tibetan language; his first mission of seven nobles was unable to find a route, and in the third year of his reign he sent Thonmi Sambhota, son of Thonmi Anu, together with sixteen companions, who, having had to overcome great difficulties on their road, reached India. There he went to Southern India, learnt the Indian characters from the Brahman Li-byin and the pundit Singhaghosha, took twenty-four of these characters with slight alterations, invented six new ones for sounds which did not exist in the Indian language, and with these formed the Tibetan capital alphabet, the Ka-phreng dbu-chan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Before returning to Tibet he translated the Karandavyuha sutra, the Avalokitesvara sutra and a number of other works, and carried back a large collection of religious works; King Srong-btsan himself soon became proficient in writing and is credited with translating several Buddhist works, and with composing instructions on horse-raising, verses and stories.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Srong-btsan sgam-po and the Chinese Princess Wen-ch'eng

region.en: Lhasa, palace on Mount Dmar-po-ri (symbolic pin at the Potala, Lhasa)
region.zh: 拉薩紅山宮（以布達拉宮為象徵定位）

texts.period: Reign of Srong-btsan sgam-po (7th century); Tibetan chronicles and Chinese T'ang annals; Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VII, using the Bodhimur, Mani bkah-hbum and T'ang annals

summary.en: When the T'ang emperor Thai-tsung refused his suit, Srong-btsan sgam-po assembled a great army, marched into Szechuan and subdued every tribe allied to China - and in 641 the emperor yielded and gave him Princess Wen-ch'eng, known in Tibetan history as Kong-cho, who brought Buddhist images and taught the 'red-faced men' the ways of the Middle Kingdom. After the marriage he built a walled city and a palace on Mount Dmar-po-ri (the later Potala), abolished the painted faces, put off felt and skins for brocade and silk, sent the sons of his chiefs to the imperial schools, and introduced silkworms, mulberries, wine-making, water-mills, paper and ink - and a law-code whipping quarrelers, beheading murderers, taxing thieves eightfold, mutilating adulterers and tearing out the tongues of perjurers.
summary.zh: 唐太宗拒婚，松贊干布遂起大軍入四川，降服諸附唐部落；貞觀十五年（641）唐室終以文成公主許嫁，藏史稱之「公主」。公主攜佛像入藏，教化「紅面之人」；松贊干布遂遷都拉薩，於紅山建宮（即後世布達拉宮），廢赭面之俗，脫氈裘而衣錦繡，遣貴族子弟入國學，並自中原引入蠶桑、造酒、水磨、紙墨，立法：鬥毆者鞭、殺人者誅、盜者八倍償、淫者刑逐、妄語者拔舌。

texts.canonical_translation: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha, London 1884 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Srong-btsan sgam-po, born about 600 AD, ascended the throne of Tibet in his thirteenth year and was recognised by the neighbouring states; his rule extended over the whole of Tibet, to the north as far as Khoten and to the east to China. Thai-tsung, the second emperor of the great T'ang dynasty, desiring doubtlessly to be on amicable terms with his warlike neighbour, sent a friendly mission to Srong-btsan, who in 634 sent a return mission and requested that the emperor would give him in marriage a princess of his family. The emperor having refused, Srong-btsan got together a great army and advanced into Szechuan, subduing all the tribes which opposed him and which were allies of the Chinese; in 641 Thai-tsung granted the request and gave him in marriage the princess Wen-ch'eng of the imperial house, known in Tibetan history as Kong-cho, or 'princess'.

Tibetan works are unanimous in affirming that Buddhism was established in the country before the advent of Wen-ch'eng, but her influence was unquestionably very great in helping to spread it; the Tibetan historian Buston says that 'in the commencement the Chinese Tcechana were the guides of the Tibetans in Buddhism'. According to the T'ang annals it was after the marriage that Srong-btsan built a walled city and erected inside its walls a palace for her residence - the event chronicled by the Tibetans as his removing his capital to Lhasa and building the palace on Mount Dmar-po-ri. As the princess disliked their custom of painting their faces red, Srong-btsan ordered his people to put a stop to the practice; he also discarded his felt and skins, put on brocade and silk, and gradually copied Chinese civilisation, sending the children of his chiefs and rich men to request admittance into the national schools to be taught the classics.

He furthermore introduced into Tibet from China silkworms and mulberry-trees, and asked the emperor for persons knowing how to make wine, water-mills, paper and ink, all of which were sent him with the calendar. He established commercial relations with the Chinese, the Minak, Hindustan, Nepal, the Hor and Guge, and extended his rule over half of Jambudvipa. A high tribunal was established to see that all laws were respected, to keep under the arrogance of the mighty and to protect the oppressed: the authors of quarrels were whipped, the murderer was put to death, the thief was made to restore eight times the value of the stolen property, the adulterer was mutilated and exiled, liars and perjurers had their tongues torn out.

The Nepalese and Chinese princesses had no children, so the king married four other women, one of whom, called Khri-cham, belonging to one of the Mon tribes which lived among the mountains between Tibet and India, bore him a son, Gung-ri gung-tsan. Srong-btsan died leaving the child-king Mang-srong under the regency of his great minister Gar; and it was in his reign that Tibet first became known among the Chinese as Thu-fan - the name which, softened through Thub-phod, 'the able ones', may be the origin of the very word Tibet.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the marriage of Songtsen Gampo and Wen-ch'eng is the founding myth of Sino-Tibetan cultural exchange; the Jowo statue she brought remains the holiest image in Lhasa. The princess as Buddhist patroness sits beside the Nepalese Bhrikuti as one of the two 'Taras' of the king.

functions: Founding charter of the Tibetan capital: Lhasa and the Dmar-po-ri palace arise from the marriage alliance
Charter of Tibetan law: the punishments of the high tribunal (whipping, beheading, eightfold restitution, mutilation, tearing out the tongue) are attributed to his reign
Explains cultural transfer from China - silkworms, mulberries, wine, water-mills, paper, ink, the calendar, the schools
Marks the turn from Bon to Buddhism in the royal cult through the princesses' images and the Nepalese connection

variants.name: Chinese T'ang annals version
variants.summary: The Chinese annals record the princess as given in 641 after Tibetan raids into Szechuan, the building of the walled city, the abolition of face-painting, and the sending of nobles' sons to the imperial schools - substantially the same as the Tibetan Bodhimur and Mani bkah-hbum, 'though greatly distorted' in Rockhill's words.

variants.name: The three suitors legend
variants.summary: The Tibetan account embellishes the marriage negotiation with three pretenders to the princess's hand - the king of Magadha, the prince of the Stag-gzig (Persians) and the ruler of the Hor (Uigurs) - competing for her before the emperor chose Songtsen Gampo.

variants.name: The Mani bkah-hbum as late construction
variants.summary: The chief work attached to Songtsen Gampo's name, a glorification of Avalokiteshvara and history of his own life, is according to Wassilieff undoubtedly modern, written by order of the Dalai Lamas to maintain their authority.

title.en: Padmasambhava and the Building of Samye

region.en: Samye monastery, south-east of Lhasa (symbolic pin at Samye)
region.zh: 拉薩東南桑耶寺（以桑耶寺為象徵定位）

texts.period: Reign of Khri-srong lde btsan (8th century); Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VII

summary.en: Khri-srong lde btsan, who did not hesitate to persecute the followers of the national Bon religion to favour Buddhist missionaries, called Shantarakshita from India; opposed, most likely by the Chinese Yogacharins, the doctor departed but advised the king to invite Padma Sambhava of Udyana, of the Madhyamika school. This celebrated teacher superintended the building of the famous Samye monastery, supposed to be a copy of the Nalanda monastery in Magadha - whose images were of pure gold when Nain Singh saw them in 1874.
summary.zh: 赤松德贊為興佛法不惜迫害苯教徒；自印度延請寂護，遭（疑為漢地瑜伽行派）反對而出藏，卻獻策請烏仗那之中觀師蓮花生入藏。蓮師監造名剎桑耶寺，相傳仿那爛陀寺之制——一八七四年拉薩所見寺中佛像皆純金。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material of living tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: He called from India Shantarakshita; but the teachings of this doctor met with so much opposition - from the Chinese Yogacharyas most likely - that he departed from Tibet, but advised the king to invite Padma Sambhava of Udyana, who belonged to the Madhyamika school of Buddhism. This celebrated teacher superintended the building of the famous Samye monastery, which is supposed to be a copy of the Nalanda monastery in Magadha; the followers of Padma Sambhava are called Urgyen-pa, an abbreviation for disciples of the man from Udyana.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

region.en: Royal hall of the Tibetan king (symbolic pin at Samye)
region.zh: 藏王御前辯場（以桑耶寺為象徵定位）

texts.period: Reign of Khri-srong lde btsan (8th century); Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VII

summary.en: After Padmasambhava's death the most popular teacher was Kamalagila, who met with great opposition from the Chinese Hwa-shang, the most influential of whom was called Mahayana or Mahadeva. Kamalagila defeated him in a grand controversy held in the king's presence, and from that time the Madhyamika doctrines were generally followed in Tibet; besides translating many Buddhist works he wrote a large number of treatises still extant in the Tengyur.
summary.zh: 蓮花生逝世後，最受敬重者為蓮花戒；他遭到漢地和尚（Hwa-shang）的強烈反對，其中以「摩訶衍那」（或摩訶提婆）最有勢力。國王御前舉行大辯論，蓮花戒折服摩訶衍，自此中觀之學遂定於一尊；他除譯經外，著述十七部仍存於丹珠爾。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: By far the most popular teacher in Tibet during this reign, after Sambhava's death, was Kamalagila. He at first met with a great deal of opposition from the Chinese Hwa-shang, the most influential of which was called Mahayana or Mahadeva; Kamalagila defeated him in a grand controversy held in the king's presence, and from that time the Madhyamika doctrines were generally followed. Besides translating a great many Buddhist works into Tibetan, he wrote a large number of treatises which are still extant in the Tengyur - in the sutra section alone seventeen works written by him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Ralpachen: The Sun-and-Moon Treaty and the Seven Tenants
title.zh: 赤祖德贊：日月盟碑與七戶養僧

region.en: Gungu Meru, the Sino-Tibetan border temple (symbolic pin at Lhasa)
region.zh: 唐蕃會盟寺（以拉薩為象徵定位）

texts.period: Reign of Ral-pa-chan (816-838 AD); Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VII

summary.en: Ralpachen concluded peace with China and had a temple erected at Gungu Meru containing a great stone slab on which sun and moon were represented, 'whereas the sun and moon moved in the heavens in friendship, so would the two kingdoms do.' Thinking the propagation of religion depended on the predominance of the clergy, he organised many classes of the priesthood, assigned to each monk a small revenue derived from five tenants, and established in the monasteries three orders of auditors, meditation and practice, with classes of elocution, controversy and exegesis - so strict that he stirred up the revolt his brother Lang Darma encouraged, and was strangled by two men at the age of forty-eight.
summary.zh: 赤祖德贊與唐修好，於界山建寺立日月盟碑：「日月行於天而和好，二國亦然。」又謂佛法之興繫於僧侶之眾，遂分僧眾為多級，每僧賜七戶供養，寺中立聽講、禪修、行持三序與講說、辯論、注疏諸科——執法過嚴，激起政變：其弟朗達瑪暗慫其事，王年四十八為二人扼殺。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: He concluded peace with China, and at Gungu Meru the Chinese and Tibetan monarchs had a temple erected in which was placed a great stone slab upon which the sun and moon were represented, and where it was written that whereas the sun and moon moved in the heavens in friendship, so would the two kingdoms do. He was the first Tibetan sovereign to pay attention to the annals of his country, recording all the events of his reign according to the Chinese system of chronology.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thinking that the propagation of religion depended much upon the predominance of the clergy, he organised many classes of the priesthood; to each monk he assigned a small revenue derived from five tenants, and established in the monasteries three orders of auditors, meditation and practice, and classes of elocution, controversy and exegesis. So strict was he in enforcing the clerical laws that he stirred up a revolt encouraged underhand by his brother Lang Darma, and the king was strangled by two men at the age of forty-eight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

region.en: Royal Tibet in the early tenth century (symbolic pin at Lhasa)
region.zh: 十世紀初的吐蕃王庭（以拉薩為象徵定位）

texts.period: Reign of Glang dar-ma (early 10th century); Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VII

summary.en: Glang Darma, 'fond of wine, a lover of field-sports, devoted to women, and, besides, cruel, tyrannical and ungracious', persecuted Buddhism so effectually that all the lamas had to flee Tibet: priests were made to use meat and intoxicating drinks, whoever kept the priesthood's way of living was banished, those who remained had to take drum and horn and follow the hounds with bow and arrows, and some were even made to learn the butcher's trade. After a few years' reign he was murdered by the Buddhist priest Dpal-gyi rdo-rje of Lha-lung.
summary.zh: 朗達瑪王「嗜酒好獵、溺於女色，殘暴專橫而無恩義」，滅法之烈令僧眾四散：迫僧食肉飲酒，守戒者流放，留者被迫擊鼓吹號、持弓箭隨獵犬出獵，甚者被迫操刀為屠。在位數年，為拉龍‧貝吉多傑（白金剛）刺殺而死。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: He appears to have persecuted Buddhism so effectually that all the lamas had to flee from Tibet: in this reign priests were made to use meat and intoxicating drinks; whoever did not give up the way of living of the priesthood was banished; some left of themselves, but those who remained had to take the drum and horn, and with bow and arrows follow the hounds in the chase - some even had to learn the butcher's trade. Glang Darma was murdered, after a few years' reign, by a Buddhist priest called Dpal-gyi rdo-rje of Lha-lung.

title.en: The Buddha's Prediction over the Lake of Li-yul
title.zh: 佛陀於于闐湖上的授記

region.en: Lake of Khoten (Li-yul), later the city of Yudan (symbolic pin at Khotan, Xinjiang)
region.zh: 于闐（李域）之湖，後為于闐城（以新疆和田為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Li-yul annals (Li-yul-gyi lo-rgyus-pa, Tengyur vol. 94), translated c. 9th century; Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VIII, translated from the Li-yul annals of the Tengyur

summary.en: In the days of the Buddha Kashyapa, Rishis who visited Li-yul were badly treated, and the vexed Nagas turned the dry country into a lake. When Shakyamuni visited with a great number of disciples he enveloped the whole lake in rays of light, from which came 363 water-lilies each with a lamp in its centre; the rays united into one which circled the lake three times to the right and disappeared in the water. Then the Buddha told Shariputra and Vaishravana to cut open the lake black as the Samangasarana mountain; Shariputra pierced it with the butt-end of his staff and Vaishravana with the end of his pike, and the Buddha foretold that within the space the light had encircled a great city would be built - the 363 lilies prefiguring the 363 Buddhist viharas of Khoten.
summary.zh: 迦葉佛世，仙人至李域為民所侮，龍王怒而使陸地化為大湖。釋迦牟尼偕大眾親至，以光明遍覆全湖，光中湧出三百六十三朵蓮花，花心各有一燈；眾光合一，繞湖右旋三匝而沒。佛命舍利弗與毗沙門天「鑿開此黑如山之湖」——尊者以杖尾刺之，天王以矛端破之——並授記：光所繞之處，將建大都城于闐；三百六十三蓮，即預示三百六十三座伽藍。

texts.language: Tibetan (translation from the Khotanese or Turkic)
texts.canonical_translation: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha, London 1884 (public domain)

narrative.en:
In the days of the Buddha Kashyapa, Li-yul was frequented by some Rishis, but they were badly treated by the people of the country, so they departed; then the Nagas were vexed, and from a dry country they converted Li-yul into a lake. When Shakyamuni was in the world he visited Li-yul in company with a great number of his disciples; the Buddha enveloped the whole of Li-yul, which was then a lake, with rays of light, and from out these rays there came 363 water-lilies, in the centre of each one of which was a lamp. Then these rays of light united into one, which circled around the lake three times, going to the right, and then disappeared in the water.

After that the Blessed One said to the Arya Shariputra and to Vaishravana, 'Cut open this lake which is as black as the Samangasarana Parvata'; then the Arya Shariputra made an opening for the lake - pierced it - with the butt-end of his staff, and Vaishravana did likewise with the end of his pike. After this the Blessed One remained for seven days for the welfare of mankind in a temple to the left-hand side of the great figure on the Gogircha mountain, where there is now a little chaitya.

While there, Ananda asked the Blessed One about what had just occurred, and the Buddha replied: from the fact that Shariputra has pierced the lake with the butt-end of his staff and Vaishravana with the end of his pike, the lake will hereafter dry up, and after my death it will be a land called Li-yul. In days to come, within the space which the light encircled three times, there will be built a great city with five towers, called U-then. The 363 lilies represented the number of Buddhist viharas which would be built in this country - an explanation which, for some unaccountable reason, the Tibetan text itself omitted, though the mountain's prodigy is preserved by Huen Thsang.

The legend belongs to a small group of Tibetan translations from the Khotanese language - the Annals of Li-yul, the Prediction of Li-yul, the Prediction of the Arhat Sanghavardhana, and the Gogringa Vyakarana preserved in the Bkah-hgyur and Bstan-hgyur - and Rockhill, editing them into chronological order and past tense, notes that these works probably reached Tibet in translation from Khotenese or Djagatai Turki. The annals supply the chronology of the prophecy's fulfilment: King Adjatasatru reigned thirty-two years, the Buddha passing away five years after his accession; from Adjatasatru to Dharmagoka there were ten generations of kings, Dharmagoka reigning fifty-four years, and two hundred and thirty-four years after the death of the Buddha there was a king of India called Dharmagoka, who in the first place had put to death many beings but had later become a righteous man through the Arhat Yasha, had confessed his sins and vowed to sin no more. At that time the lake had dried up, but Li-yul was still uninhabited - the country waiting, as the annals frame it, for the child who would be suckled by the earth to grow up and claim it.",
        "notes": "Cultural function: the Khotanese Buddhist annals recast the nation's origin as a fulfilled Buddha-prediction - the standard move Rockhill notes for countries adopting Buddhism - binding city-site, monastery-count and lake-draining to the person of the historical Buddha."

functions: Founding charter of Khoten: the city-site is the very circle of the Buddha's thrice-circling light
Explains the local geography as the residue of a sacred act - the lake drained by Shariputra's staff and Vaishravana's pike
Turns a hostile landscape (the Nagas' lake) into an ordination of the Buddhist future: 363 lilies, 363 monasteries
Legitimates the guardian cult of Vaishravana in the oasis-kingdom

variants.name: Huen Thsang's version
variants.summary: The Chinese pilgrim preserves substantially the same legend - the mountain there called Gogringa - and adds the detail of the 363 lilies as the number of viharas; Abel Remusat's Histoire de la Ville de Khotan reproduces it from Chinese sources.

title.en: Kusthana, Suckled by the Earth: The Founding of Khoten

region.en: Valley of the U-then river, Khoten (symbolic pin at Khotan, Xinjiang)
region.zh: 于闐河谷（以新疆和田為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Li-yul annals (Tengyur vol. 94), translated c. 9th century; Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VIII

summary.en: King Dharmagoka's consort bears a son whom the soothsayers doom to reign while his father lives; abandoned on the earth, the child is fed by a breast that rises from the ground - Kusthana, 'breast of the earth'. The childless ruler of China, praying to Vaishravana for a thousandth son, has the waif carried off and reared as his own; taunted by his foster-brothers and confirmed by the annals, Kusthana leaves with ten thousand men, meets in the west the seven thousand exiles of the Indian minister Yasha, and the two hosts quarrel over the site until Vaishravana and Shrimahadevi appear and are enshrined as the chief guardians of the realm - so the Chinese settle the lower river, the Indians the upper, and Khoten becomes a nation half Chinese, half Indian, speaking a dialect that is neither.
summary.zh: 法阿育王（Dharmagoka）之后生子，相者言其「在父在位時即將為王」，王懼而命棄之；棄兒得大地所生之乳哺養不死，故名「地乳」（Kusthana）。無子的中國王祈毗沙門天賜千子之末，此兒被攜往中原撫養；兄弟譏其非王種，查史證實，遂率萬人西行，與印度大臣耶舍七千放逐者相遇——兩軍爭地不和，毗沙門天與吉祥天女現身，遂各建廟祀之，尊為國之主護。華人居河下，印度人居河上，雜處其間——李域從此半華半印，語言亦非華非印。

texts.canonical_translation: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha, London 1884 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Two hundred and thirty-four years after the death of the Buddha there was a king of India called Dharmagoka, who in the first place had put to death many beings but had later become a righteous man through the Arhat Yasha, having confessed his sins and vowed to sin no more. In the thirtieth year of his reign his queen-consort brought forth a son; the soothsayers, being summoned, declared that the child bore many marks of greatness and that he would be king during his father's lifetime. Then the king, fearing that this child would dethrone him, gave orders that he should be abandoned; and the mother, apprehending that if the child were not abandoned the king would have him put to death, did as he had ordered. But when the child had been abandoned, there arose a breast on the earth from which he derived sustenance, so that he did not die - for this reason he was called Kusthana, 'breast of the earth'.

Now at that time there lived a ruler of Rgya (China), a great Bodhisattva, who had 999 sons and had prayed to Vaishravana that he might have one more to complete the thousand. Vaishravana looked about, and perceiving that the little waif Kusthana was a promising person, carried him off and made him the son of the ruler of Rgya. The ruler brought him up, but one day, while quarrelling with the children of the king of Rgya, they said to Kusthana, 'thou art not the son of the sovereign of Rgya.' He was distressed, and having ascertained from other men that this statement was borne out by the annals of Rgya, he asked the king to allow him to go seek his native land; and though the king told him many times, 'thou art my son; this is thy native land; be not thus distressed', yet he hearkened not.

Kusthana wanted a kingdom for himself; he got together a host of 10,000 men and went to seek a home in the west, coming to Me-skar of Li-yul. Meanwhile Yasha, the minister of Raja Dharmagoka, had so extended his family influence that his relatives became obnoxious to the king, and he left the country with 7,000 men, seeking a home to the west and the east, until he came into the country below the river of U-then. Two traders from among Kusthana's followers ran away in their slippers and, though there was no road, came to To-la; from the fact that they had walked with slippers on, this country received its name. Seeing a goodly tract of uninhabited land, they thought, 'this will do for a home for Prince Kusthana', and visited the encampment of the minister Yasha, who sent a message to Me-skar: thou being of royal family and I of ministerial family, let us here unite and establish ourselves in this district of U-then, and thou shalt be king and I minister.

The prince and the minister could not agree where to locate their home, their hosts were divided, and they commenced to quarrel - but Vaishravana and Shrimahadevi having appeared to them, they built on that very spot a temple to each one of these gods, and from that day forth honoured Vaishravana and Shrimahadevi as the chief guardians of the realm. Reconciled, the prince was made king and the minister, minister; the Chinese followers of Kusthana were established on the lower side of the U-then river, the Indian followers of Yasha on the upper bank, and between the two they settled the Indians and Chinese indiscriminately, building a fortress. Li being a country half Chinese and half Indian, the dialect of the people is neither Indian nor Chinese; the letters resemble closely those of India, the habits of the people are very similar to those of China, and the religion and the sacred language are very similar to those of India. Kusthana was twelve years old when he gave up the princely estate of the ruler of Rgya, and was aged nineteen when he founded the kingdom of Li-yul - counting exactly from the nirvana of the Buddha, 234 years had elapsed.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the Khotanese annals turn the ethnic mixture of the oasis into a charter - the bilingual, bi-cultural nation is founded by a rejected child nourished by the land itself, and its guardian deities appear precisely to stop a civil war.

functions: Founding charter of Khoten's dual (Sino-Indian) nationhood, explained through two hosts settled on opposite banks
Explains the oasis's hybrid language and scripts as the natural product of the founding population
Establishes the guardian cult of Vaishravana and Shrimahadevi as the divinities who stopped the founding quarrel
Recasts an unwanted royal child as the destined city-founder, suckled by the earth itself

variants.name: Huen Thsang's version
variants.summary: The Chinese pilgrim's account is easily made to agree with the Tibetan by suppressing the part which precedes Kusthana's arrival in China; the Gogringa recension gives the earth-breast story with the name 'Suckled from the earth' (Sa-las nu-ma nu).

title.en: The King Who Would Not Sound the Ganta

region.en: Tsu-la grove of Tsar-ma, Khoten (symbolic pin at Khotan)
region.zh: 于闐乍瑪林苑（以和田為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Li-yul annals (Tengyur vol. 94); Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VIII

summary.en: One hundred and sixty-five years after the founding of Khoten, Vijayasambhava - an incarnation of Maitreya and Manjushri - ascended the throne, and the Dharma was first introduced into Li-yul. The Arya Vairochana, assuming the form of a Bhikshu, dwelt in the Tsu-la grove, taught the ignorant cattle-herders in the Li language, and invented the characters of Li. When the vihara was finished and the king was told to sound the ganta, he answered: may I never sound the ganta unless the Tathagata comes here and gives me one! - and immediately Vairochana assumed the appearance of the Tathagata, taught like the Tathagata, and gave the king a ganta which he sounded without ceasing for seven days.
summary.zh: 李域建國後一百六十五年，毘耶耶娑婆訶（彌勒與文殊化身）登位，佛法始入其國。聖者毘盧遮那化為比丘，住乍瑪林苑，以李語教化無知的牧牛人，並創製李文。寺成之日，王被告知鳴鈴聚眾，王答：「若非如來親臨賜鈴，我終不擊鈴！」毘盧遮那即刻現如來相，說法如佛，賜王以鈴——王擊鈴七日不輟。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Vijayasambhava was an incarnation of Maitreya and Manjushri; having assumed the form of a Bhikshu, the Arya Vairochana came and dwelt in the Tsu-la grove in the country of Tsar-ma, became the spiritual guide of the inhabitants of Li-yul, taught the ignorant cattle-herders in the Li language, and invented the characters of Li - after this the Dharma appeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: King Vijayasambhava built the great vihara of Tsar-ma, but he greatly longed for some relics of the body of the Tathagata; he was told to build a chaitya, and when the vihara was finished, Vairochana told the king to sound the ganta and to invite the Aryas. He replied, may I never sound the ganta unless the Tathagata comes here and gives me a ganta! Immediately Vairochana assumed the appearance of the Tathagata, and after having taught like the Tathagata sixty great dharmas at Tsar-ma, he gave King Vijayasambhava a ganta, and the king sounded it without ceasing for seven days.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Chinese Princess and the Stolen Silkworms of Khoten
title.zh: 和闐公主與偷渡的蠶種

region.en: Snake-raising house of Ma-dza, Khoten (symbolic pin at Khotan)
region.zh: 和闐麻闍養蠶房（以和田為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Li-yul annals (Tengyur vol. 94); Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VIII

summary.en: King Vijayajaya married the Chinese princess Pu-nye-shar, who wished to introduce silkworms into Li-yul; the Chinese ministers led the king to believe the worms would become venomous snakes ravaging the land, and he ordered the snake-raising house burnt down. The queen saved some and reared them secretly until she could put on silk garments; showing them to the king, she explained everything, and he, greatly regretting what he had done, called the Bhikshu Sanghaghosha from India to be his spiritual adviser, and built chaityas and a great vihara to atone for his wickedness.
summary.zh: 毘耶耶闍王娶漢公主蒲尼夏；公主欲於李域興蠶桑，中國大臣卻誘使國王相信蠶將化為毒蛇為害全境，王遂下令焚毀「養蛇房」。公主私藏蠶種祕密飼養，待織成絲衣後向國王出示並說明一切；王大悔，迎印度僧伽霍沙為師，並建塔造大寺以贖前罪。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation. Parallel recorded by Huen Thsang with the princess named Lou-tche.

passages.text: King Vijayajaya married the daughter of the ruler of Rgya, Princess Pu-nye-shar; desiring to introduce silkworms into Li-yul she commenced raising some at Ma-dza, but the ministers of China, having led the king to believe that these worms would become venomous snakes which would ravage the land, he gave orders to have the snake-raising house burnt down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The queen, however, managed to save some and reared them secretly; when after a time she had procured silk and raw silk, she put on silk garments, showed them to the king and explained the whole thing, and he greatly regretted what he had done. He called from India the Bhikshu Sanghaghosha and made him his spiritual adviser, and to atone for his wickedness in having destroyed the greater part of the silkworms he built the chaityas and a great vihara of Ma-dza.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Exodus of the Bhikshus from Li-yul

region.en: Road from Khoten through the highlands to Tibet (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自于闐越高原入藏之路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Li-yul annals (late 9th century AD); Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VIII

summary.en: Fifteen hundred years after the Buddha's death the king of Li-yul was an unbeliever who persecuted the clergy; wars and diseases raged, unseasonable frosts, insects, birds and mice devastated the fields, and unbelieving ministers seized the viharas. The Bhikshus assembled at the Tsar-ma vihara where the Dharma had first been preached, confessed, and decided to leave for Tibet where the Triratna was honoured. A believing king of the winds threw down a cairn and disclosed a golden vase full of pearls; the Nagas showed them one of gold-dust; and when they lost their way at a cross-road, Vaishravana assumed the appearance of a loaded white yak and led them four or five days to Ts'al-byi in Tibet - where the king, seventh successor of Songtsen Gampo, built seven viharas for them.
summary.zh: 佛滅一千五百年後，李域王不信法而迫害僧團：刀兵疾疫、寒暑失調、蟲鳥鼠害，田疇盡毀，僧舍為不信之王臣所奪。眾僧會於佛法初興的乍瑪寺懺悔，決意遷往敬信三寶之吐蕃。信法風王推倒石堆，得滿缽珍珠；龍王又示金瓶金砂；迷途之際，毗沙門天化作負重的白犛牛引路四五日，直至藏地擦爾域——贊普為之建寺七座。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Each succeeding year was worse than the previous one; wars and diseases raged, untimely winds and rains befell them, unseasonable frosts, insects, birds and mice devastated their fields, and unbelieving ministers in Li-yul violently took possession of the abodes of the Bhikshus. Then the Bhikshus assembled in the Tsar-ma vihara, in which the Dharma had first been preached in this country, and after confession decided to leave the country and turn their steps toward Bod-yul, for they had heard that the Triratna was honoured in that land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the Yeshes-ri vihara they found in the ruins of an old chaitya a great golden vase full of pearls, exchanged its contents for grain, and at the Chang vihara the Nagas disclosed to them a golden vase full of gold-dust; at the Stong-nya vihara Vaishravana and Shrimahadevi transformed themselves into a man and woman of that country and entertained the clergy for a fortnight, giving them at departure a bag full of gold pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coming to a cross-road in the country of the red-faced men, they got into a lateral valley and lost their way; then Vaishravana assumed the appearance of a loaded white yak and the Bhikshus followed after it, thinking that it would take them to where men lived. He led them for four or five days until they reached Ts'al-byi in Tibet, and then he vanished; the inhabitants sent word to the king of Bod-yul, and the king, at the queen's request, had built for them seven viharas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Elapatra, the Naga Who Made Himself a Bridge
title.zh: 以蛇身為橋的龍王伊羅鉢多羅

region.en: Great lake between Tibet and Gandhara (symbolic pin in the western Himalaya)
region.zh: 吐蕃與健馱邏間之大湖（以西喜馬拉雅為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Li-yul annals (Prediction of Sanghavardhana, Tengyur vol. 94), translated c. 9th century; Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VIII

summary.en: When the expelled Bhikshus were pursued by Tibetan troops and halted at a great lake with provisions for only fifteen days against a forty-five-day march, the Naga king Elapatra, taking the shape of an old man, counted their stores and told them the way was blocked; and then, kneeling before them - 'weep not, for the Sangha I will sacrifice my life; I will bridge this lake over with my body' - he became an enormous serpent, his fore-parts encircling a Tibetan mountain-top and his tail a mountain in Gandhara, a bridge wide enough for five waggons abreast. The fugitives crossed, the skin of his back torn by hoofs and feet until blood and matter flowed; when all had passed, the Naga king died, the lake dried up, his remains stayed there like a mountain - and in days to come the Buddha Maitreya will come that way, and Elapatra, having finished his series of births, will then obtain Arhatship.
summary.zh: 被逐的僧侶遭吐蕃兵追趕，困於大湖之畔——存糧僅十五日，而繞湖至健馱邏須行四十五日。龍王伊羅鉢多羅化作老翁前來，一問一答之後，跪而言曰：「勿泣！我願為僧團獻身，以身為橫湖之橋。」遂化巨蟒，前半身繞吐蕃山頂，尾纏健馱邏山巔，橋寬可容五車並行。眾人踐背而過，龍背之皮被蹄足剝裂，膿血迸流，誤入者立死。眾人既過，龍王死，湖水涸，其屍如山——彌勒佛將率五百弟子行經此地，屆時伊羅鉢多羅歷劫圓滿，得阿羅漢果。

texts.canonical_translation: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha, London 1884 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Then all the Bhikshus started out for Mahagandhara in the west, and it being then a time of war and trouble, the Bhikshus of India also started for Gandhara, so that down to the Ganges there was an end of following the Dharma. Then the troops of Bod-yul hurried in pursuit of the Bhikshus, who came to a great lake. Then the Naga king Elapatra took the shape of an old man and went to the Bhikshus and asked them where they were going. 'We have lost in an unbelieving land all means of subsistence,' they replied, 'and we are now on our way to Gandhara, where we hope to find the necessaries of life.' Elapatra asked them what provisions they had, and when they had accurately counted all that they had among them, they told him that they had provisions for fifteen days. 'From here to Gandhara,' replied the Naga king, 'requires forty-five days, and you must go around this lake; how can you manage with fifteen days' provisions? Moreover, the intervening country is very elevated, thickly wooded, infested with wild beasts, venomous serpents, and brigands.'

Then the Bhikshus, both male and female, gave way to grief, for they thought that their last hour was nigh. But Elapatra, kneeling down before them, said, 'Weep not; for the Sangha I will sacrifice my life; I will bridge this lake over with my body.' Then he took the shape of an enormous serpent, and made a bridge wide enough for five waggons to pass abreast, with the fore part of his body encircling the top of a mountain in Bod, and with his tail wrapped around the top of a mountain in Gandhara. The fugitive Bhikshus passed the lake on this bridge, but the skin on the back of the Naga king was torn off by the hoofs of the cattle and the men's feet, so that it made a great wound, from which flowed matter and blood, and any of the men or beasts who fell into this wound died from it. When every one had passed over, the Naga king died, and the lake drying up, his remains stayed there like unto a mountain. In days to come the Buddha Maitreya will come that way with his 500 disciples; Elapatra, having finished his series of births, will then obtain the reward of Arhatship. The same annals carry the fugitives on into Gandhara, where the believing king's death divided the kingdom between two warring sons, a thousand resolute Sramaneras set a believer on the throne, murdered him after five months, made a Bhikshu king for two years - and were then slaughtered with all the monks of Gandhara by the nobles, so that those alone escaped who fled to Mid-India; down to the Ganges, the annals say, there was an end of following the Dharma. The Naga's sacrifice thus closes not a rescue but an age - the bridge is the last road of the Dharma's old geography, and its mountain-remnant a relic already waiting for Maitreya's future with his five hundred disciples.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the exodus legend of the Li-yul annals makes the land-bridge between the two Buddhist countries the sacrifice of a serpent-king - the landscape itself is the wound of the Sangha's passage - and attaches the story to Maitreya's future, so the geography is eschatological.

functions: Explains the mountain-remnant left by a vanished lake as the body of a sacrificed guardian
Charter of sanctuary: the Buddhist lands are bound by a serpent-king who dies for the Sangha
Binds the legend to Maitreya's future coming, so the western passes themselves await redemption
Turns the persecution of the monks from Li-yul and Tibet into one continuous epic of exile

variants.name: Elapatra in the Buddha's lifetime
variants.text_tradition: Dulva xi. f. 118; the Kandayana episode
variants.summary: The same Naga appears in the Tibetan Vinaya residing at Takshasila in the Buddha's time - the annals note that he had apparently changed his residence since days of old.

title.en: The Mirror for the Noseless: The Kaushambi Massacre

region.en: Vihara of Kaushambi, Mid-India (symbolic pin at Kaushambi, India)
region.zh: 中印度憍賞彌伽藍（以憍賞彌為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Li-yul annals (late 9th century AD); Rockhill's English 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. VIII

summary.en: The penitent king Durdarga, born under a rain of blood with blood-red hands marked on his breast, invited all the Bhikshus of Jambudvipa - 200,000 - to confess daily; but when the Tripitaka-master Shringaka was called on to repeat the Pratimoksha Sutra, he answered: what can the Pratimoksha do for you? What is the good of a looking-glass for a man whose nose and ears are cut off? - and the Arhat Surata rebuked him for speaking to men whole as the Sugata ordained. His enraged disciple killed the Arhat with a door-bar; the Arhat's disciple killed Shringaka with a stick; the two camps of Bhikshus killed each other - and at dawn the king pressed the corpses to his breast, weeping, as the Trayastrimcat Devas were defeated by the Asuras and fell to lower heavens.
summary.zh: 誕生時天降血雨、胸前印有血手印的懺悔王多爾達爾嘎，延請閻浮提二十萬比丘齊聚憍賞彌日日懺悔。三藏法師輸羅伽迦被請誦《別解脫經》，卻答：「《別解脫》於汝何益？無鼻無耳之人，照鏡何用！」羅漢蘇囉吒叱之「我等完具，如佛所制」，其弟子怒以門閂殺羅漢，羅漢弟子又以杖殺輸羅伽迦——兩營比丘自相殘殺。黎明王抱屍痛哭，而此時三十三天為阿修羅所敗，天人墮於無想諸天——佛法將滅，天界亦暗。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Durdarga, wishing to atone for all his sins, invited a Bhikshu called Shringaka, learned in the Tripitaka, and was told that as a penance he must entertain all the Bhikshus of Jambudvipa and daily confess his sins before them; the king invited all the Bhikshus throughout India, and they, rejoicing, gathered together in Kaugambi to the number of 200,000.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the night of the fifteenth day of the month the Bhikshus called upon Shringaka to repeat the Pratimoksha Sutra, but he answered, what can the Pratimoksha do for you? What is the good of a looking-glass for a man whose nose and ears are cut off? Then an Arhat called Surata arose and cried with a lion's voice, why speak you thus? I am whole as the Sugata ordained - and the enraged disciple of Shringaka seized a door-bar and killed the Arhat; the Arhat's disciple killed Shringaka, and all the Bhikshus, dividing into two camps, killed each other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: At dawn the king saw all the Bhikshus lying dead, and his eyes were obscured with tears; he rushed to the vihara calling their names and pressed their corpses to his breast, crying, alas, Tripitaka! thou didst possess the treasure of the Dharma of the Sugata! And as the shades of night were closing around the blessed law, the Trayastrimcat Devas were defeated by the Asuras and fled, and transmigrating passed among the Asandjasattva Devas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
